title: What the BRICS Summit Meant for Brazil
gist: Catherine Osborn argues Brazil kept U.N. and Paris climate language alive in the New Delhi BRICS declaration, but its ability to steer an expanded, more anti-Western bloc may end if Flávio Bolsonaro wins Brazil's Oct. 4 election. The brief also flags Iran-war spillovers in Latin America: Panama Canal transit cuts with record prices as Asian buyers source U.S. Gulf energy, and fuel-price unrest in Guatemala.

insights.claim: BRICS cooperation is deepening as the global order unravels; many demands such as U.N. Security Council expansion have not materialized, but the bloc has steadily expanded economic ties, including its own development bank.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: BRICS economic integration, not grand political reform, is the channel to monitor for trade and financing shifts.

insights.claim: Brazil opposed BRICS expansion from five to nine members in 2024, fearing loss of cohesion with anti-West Iran, and like India wants the bloc to be reformist rather than revolutionary.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Internal BRICS divisions limit its capacity to act as a unified anti-Western economic bloc.
insights.locator: Brazil, a founding member of BRICS

insights.claim: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian attended the New Delhi BRICS summit, his furthest trip since the Iran war began in February, alongside an Emirati delegation led by Abu Dhabi's crown prince despite the two sides being at war.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: BRICS is a rare venue where Iran-war belligerents meet, a possible diplomatic channel.
insights.locator: BRICS members have long sought to reform

insights.claim: Brazilian Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira stood in for Lula, and Brazil secured a BRICS declaration reaffirming support for the U.N. system and the Paris climate agreement, going further than the G-7, whose latest declarations omitted the climate pact.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Emerging-market blocs are now more pro-climate-framework than the G-7, relevant for climate-finance flows.
insights.quote: a multipolar world that promises peace and prosperity must not be confused with a world of spheres of influence.
insights.locator: Brazilian Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira attended

insights.claim: Russia's begrudging agreement to acknowledge the legitimacy of the U.N. system at BRICS bodes better for the U.N.'s future functioning than a block would have, as U.N. leadership is up for grabs.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Marginal signal on multilateral institutions' survival during the U.N. leadership contest.
insights.locator: Russia may have only begrudgingly endorsed

insights.claim: Brazil's window to steer BRICS may close with the Oct. 4 general election, where far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, whose camp has a record of U.N.-bashing and climate denial, has as strong a chance of winning as Lula, according to polls.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: A coin-flip Brazilian election is a major binary for Brazilian assets, climate policy and BRICS direction; position for volatility around Oct. 4.
insights.locator: Brazil’s window to continue shaping BRICS

insights.claim: Panama plans to cut Panama Canal transits to an average 29.5 vessels per day from October, down 18 percent from August, because of an El Niño-worsened drought.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Tighter canal capacity raises freight rates and transit times for U.S.-Asia LNG, LPG and container routes.

insights.claim: Panama Canal transit prices are climbing to record highs as Asian energy importers shift from Persian Gulf supplies to U.S. Gulf Coast cargoes that must pass through Panama amid the Iran war.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Iran war is structurally boosting U.S. Gulf energy exports to Asia while raising canal-dependent shipping costs; watch canal auction prices and U.S. export volumes.

insights.claim: Guatemala has joined countries where Iran-war economic fallout became unrest, with gas prices topping $6 per gallon and highway blockades for over a week; President Bernardo Arévalo's decree to cap fuel prices was blocked in Congress.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Fuel-price protests are spreading across import-dependent EMs; watch for subsidy costs and political instability in Central America.

insights.claim: Guatemala's moneyed establishment lobbied Trump against Arévalo's anti-corruption agenda, and the administration reportedly boosted judicial candidates accused of corruption; Arévalo now has the lowest approval among Latin American leaders in a CB Global Data poll.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Weakening reformist governance raises Guatemala's institutional and political risk.
insights.locator: Reformers had high hopes that Arévalo

themes.theme: Latin American democracy and U.S.-China views

insights.claim: Vanderbilt's AmericasBarometer found support for democracy in Latin America rose to 65 percent from 59 percent in 2023, linked to improving lived experiences with crime, corruption and economic well-being.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Rising democratic support alongside better economic conditions modestly lowers regional political-risk premia.
insights.locator: Support for democracy on the rise

insights.claim: Views of China in Latin America are improving relative to the United States, as democracy promotion has largely fallen off Washington's agenda under Trump.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Improving Chinese standing supports deeper Chinese trade and investment in Latin America.
insights.locator: The survey also touched on geopolitics
